slides:
When she says
“I’m exhausted.”

5 replies to try when your partner
has had a hard day.

“Do you want me
to listen, or help
you think it through?”

Ask what kind of support she wants
before offering a solution.

“What can I take
off your plate
tonight?”

Offer something specific: dinner,
the dishes, or the next errand.

“You don’t have to
explain it perfectly.”

Leave room for a pause.
Let her find her words.

“I noticed how
much you handled
today.”

Name the effort you actually saw.
Keep the appreciation honest.

“Want company,
or a little quiet?”

Let her choose.
Respect the answer.
bondify.caption:
When your partner has had a long day, try asking what would help.

These are conversation ideas, not a formula. Use the words that sound like you, and listen to the answer.

Save this for the evening when you want to help but cannot find the words.

#CouplesCommunication #HealthyRelationships #Marriage #RelationshipAdvice #EmotionalConnection

slides:
A full calendar.
But room for
what matters?

A study reflection on
Good, Better, Best.

Good things can
compete for the
same hour.

Elder Oaks invites us to consider which
choices deepen faith and family connection.

What deserves
your best attention
this week?

Our reflection prompt:
Name one relationship or spiritual practice.

Choose one thing.
Make room for it.

Our application idea:
Set aside a specific time for that priority.

Read. Reflect.
Then make
one choice.

Good, Better, Best
Dallin H. Oaks · October 2007

Study notes and application, not direct quotations.
lds-conference.caption:
A full schedule can still leave little time for your priorities.

In Good, Better, Best, Elder Dallin H. Oaks asks us to consider how our choices strengthen faith in Jesus Christ and our families.

Our study prompt: what will you make room for this week?

Source: Good, Better, Best — October 2007 General Conference.

slides:
Does your app
need that
extra feature?

A small checklist for
your next build decision.

Name the job
before the feature.

Write one sentence:
“This helps someone do ___.”

Picture the
moment of use.

Where are they?
What are they trying to finish?

Find the
smallest useful
version.

What can you remove while still
letting someone finish that job?

Put it in front
of someone.

Ask them to try the task.
Notice where they hesitate.

Keep the feature
that earns
its place.

Save this checklist for
your next scope decision.
kelvintanzy.caption:
Before adding another feature, give it one clear job.

Who is it for? When will they use it? What should they be able to finish?

Then put the smallest useful version in front of someone and watch where they get stuck.

Which feature are you deciding whether to build?
